title: Building a timber hay rack
subtitle: A fixed hay rack reduces waste significantly compared to throwing hay on the ground. Sheep and goats pull it free faster than they can eat it otherwise.
excerpt: A basic wall-mounted hay rack takes an afternoon to build and lasts years. It holds a small bale section off the ground so animals eat rather than stand on the hay. The design here suits sheep, goats, or a mixed pen: vertical timber slats wide enough for a muzzle to reach through, but not so wide that heads can become caught.
sourceNotes: John Seymour, The New Complete Book of Self-Sufficiency (2003), farm equipment chapter. Practical Farmer magazine (historical UK editions), hay rack construction. General livestock pen design references, Farmers Weekly archive. Standard timber construction practice, UK.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fixed or portable frame that holds hay off the ground for livestock to eat. Reduces wastage caused by animals standing on or defecating in floor-fed hay. A fixed wall-mounted rack is standard for permanent housing.

content.text: uses three components: two side frames, a series of vertical slats, and a back board to mount it to the wall. The dimensions below suit a single adult sheep or goat using the rack alone; double the width for a shared pen with up to four animals.

attrs.title: Cut list — single rack, 60 cm wide

content.text: 2 × side frame uprights: 75 × 50 mm treated timber, 80 cm long
2 × side frame horizontals: 75 × 50 mm treated timber, 40 cm long
7 × slats: 50 × 25 mm treated timber, 70 cm long
1 × back board: 150 × 25 mm treated timber, 60 cm long (for wall fixing)
Exterior grade screws, 50 mm and 65 mm

Build each side frame first: screw the two horizontals between the two uprights to make a rectangle 80 cm high and 40 cm deep. The lower horizontal sits 30 cm from the base (to catch any dropped hay); the upper horizontal sits 10 cm from the top.

Attach the slats across the front of the two side frames, spaced evenly across the 60 cm width. With 7 slats at 50 mm wide, the gaps are approximately 60 mm, wide enough for a sheep's muzzle to reach through, not wide enough to trap a head.
Attach the back board across the top of both side frames, flush at the back. This board is the fixing point to the wall.
Apply exterior wood preservative to all cut ends, particularly the base of the uprights where moisture collects.

Mount the rack to the wall at 80-90 cm height (measured to the bottom of the rack from the floor). This height suits both sheep and goats without them having to stretch uncomfortably or lower their heads far enough to inhale dust.

Check the fixings annually. The slats take heavy lateral pressure as animals pull hay and the screws work loose over time. Re-treat the cut timber ends every two years. A rack in a covered building will last 10 years or more; one in an outdoor run exposed to rain needs more frequent checks.
